<think>The user asks: "Explain the Ship of Theseus paradox and how a modern philosopher might resolve it."

We need to respond with an accessible explanation of the paradox, then discuss possible modern philosophical resolutions, referencing various theories: metaphysics (essentialism, four-dimensionalism, perdurantism), identity criteria, psychological continuity, functionalism, material composition, mereology, etc. Also mention the role of vagueness and sorites paradox, the problem of gradual change vs. sudden change. Mention the modern analytic tradition: David Lewis on perdurantism, David Wiggins, Peter van Inwagen, the problem of the Ship of Theseus as an instance of the problem of the persistence of objects. Also mention that modern philosophers might resolve it by appealing to the concept of "object" as a social construct, or by employing a "stage ontology" where objects are spatiotemporal parts (worms). Also mention that the resolution may involve a combination of essentialism and the idea that identity is not strict but a matter of degree. Also mention the "paradox of the ship of Theseus" as a thought experiment used to illustrate the problem of persistence through time, and the modern solutions: (1) perdurantism (objects are four-dimensional worms, and the ship is a temporal part of a larger "ship worm" that includes all stages; the original ship and the rebuilt ship are both parts of the same worm). (2) endurantism (objects wholly exist at each time; the ship persists as the same object if it has the right sort of continuity). (3) essentialism (the ship has essential properties that are preserved, e.g., being a ship, being a vessel, etc.). (4) The "no identity across time" view (objects are not strictly identical over time; we can talk about approximate identity or "is the same ship" as a matter of convention). (5) The "social/linguistic" resolution: the term "ship" is a kind of sortal concept; identity conditions are given by the sortal, and we can decide that the ship is the same if it continues to satisfy the sortal's criteria.
